newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Salvation Army bell-ringers may soon take plastic.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Salvation Army bell-ringers may soon take plastic.

text.p: Holiday shoppers may soon lack the excuse of empty pockets to avoid donating money to Salvation Army bell-ringers. By next Christmas, donors in some places may be able to say, "Charge it!"

For the first time, donors in one experimental U.S. location can charge their gifts in streetcorner kettles to credit cards this year. As that spreads, and as the Salvation Army launches an Internet site next year, the charity will be thrust into the 21st century in its 105th year.

With record donations expected this year, it appears that the red kettle is here to stay. The credit-card version, being tested at Chapel Hill Mall in Akron, Ohio, has a magnetic strip mounted on the traditional kettle through which donors slide their cards. They then punch in the contribution amount on a keypad and a receipt spits out of the coin slot.

Salvation Army Major Francis Kirk in Akron says that although they have not gathered any figures yet, the credit card kettle is a success. "People seem to be pleased with it," he said. "It provides a convenience for the donor."

He also said the computerized kettle allows people to make larger donations than they would if paying cash. He plans to add a couple more in Akron next year and other Salvation Army offices have also expressed interest.
The credit card kettle was created by Akron-based Telxon Corporation, which gave the local Salvation Army the test kettle free of charge. Future models will cost about $3,000.

The Salvation Army is planning to become even more hi-tech next year, with plans to develop an Internet site on the World Wide Web, James Bradley, director of national communications at the Alexandria, Virginia, based charity, said. The national page will join more than a dozen local Salvation Army home pages already on the Web.

The charity hopes to take in $70 million in its nearly 20,000 kettles this year, up from $66.4 million last year. Combined with the annual mail campaign, it brought in $198.5 million in the United States last year just over the holidays, and $1.4 billion in all of 1995.

Acting as the "evangelical part" of the Universal Christian Church, the Salvation Army uses the kettle money to provide holiday meals and toys, rent and utility payments and counselling and rehabilitation services throughout the year. It estimates that 6.8 million people benefited from funds raised by the kettle programme last year.

The Salvation Army was founded by William Booth in 1865 in London. The first kettles appeared in 1891 on a ferry landing in San Francisco after a Salvation Army captain decided to raise money to provide Christmas dinner to the poor.

The army had always relied almost totally on volunteers, but in recent years the kettle programme has had to hire more paid workers. About 30 percent of this year's 1 million bell ringers are actually being paid due to a lack of volunteers.

"Frankly, people have jobs," said John-Joseph van Haelewyn, public relations director for the Salvation Army in Washington and Virginia. While costly, he said, hiring kettle attendants provides jobs for many poor people who are themselves Salvation Army beneficiaries.

Diane Gaston, 49, said she is working 6 days a week as a bell ringer in Washington for the second year to raise money for herself and her nieces and nephews. "For the Christmas money, it's worth it," she said as she shifted from foot to foot, trying to keep warm at her post by a downtown Washington department store.

Although the kettle programme is going high-tech, it appears that the traditional spirit of giving is still alive. Every year someone donates four $500 bills in a California kettle. Once someone dropped in an engagement ring. This year, a wadded-up pack of bills -- nearly $1,400 -- turned up in a kettle in Alexandria, Virginia, van Haelewyn said.
But it is the small donations that make the difference.
"The thing that's amazing to me is that they get as much money as they do from nickels and coins," Bradley said. "It all adds up."
